A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Equivariant Splitting work. Their main texts and Appendices A-C are readable, and corresponding methods, proofs, tables and figures can be reliably matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments on MNIST, DIV2K and FastMRI, including architectural ablations and additional noisy MRI results in Appendix B.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds CT, acquired MRI measurements, structured-mask and unknown-noise experiments, MAP simulations and training-time measurements.

M1.justification: The ES and noisy R2R objectives, equivariant reconstructor definition, architectures and split-averaged inference remain unchanged. Algorithms 1-2 document the existing procedure. Testing the existing noiseless loss on noisy measurements does not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: v4 adds LIDC-IDRI sparse-view CT simulations and acquired FastMRI k-space measurements to v1's coverage (Sections 5.3-5.4). Appendix B also adds noisy inpainting with random and periodic column masks and a Gaussian-prior decimation simulation, substantially expanding acquisition conditions and test scenarios.

E2.justification: FBP is newly evaluated as a CT comparator in v4 Table 1. Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged, including the pseudo-inverse baseline already present in v1 Figure 4. Most added evaluations reuse existing comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include 50-view CT with noise standard deviation 0.001 and a 900/110 training/test split, sinc resampling of acquired MRI data, controlled use of noiseless ES/EI losses on noisy data, and a 256-sample MAP equivariance test. These are added evaluation designs; retained benchmark splits and metrics remain stable.

E4.justification: v1's architectural ablations, noise-dominated MRI comparisons and training curves are retained. v4 adds structured-mask tests probing failure under near-equivariant operators, known-versus-unknown noise comparisons, empirical MAP-equivariance verification and computational-cost analysis (Tables 7-10). These substantially broaden the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Both versions report reconstruction scores using averages and standard deviations. v4 introduces no repeated-training run counts, seed disclosures, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures. The 256 samples in its MAP experiment specify evaluation sample size rather than repeated training.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark values agree, including v1 Table 5 matched to v4 Table 6 apart from equivalent rounding. New results include CT PSNR of 32.62 for ES versus 28.61 for EI, and acquired-MRI PSNR of 28.30 versus 27.88 (Table 1). Table 7 exposes periodic-mask failure, while Table 8 shows ES below EI under unknown high MRI noise: 25.73 versus 26.02. These are newly reported results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The main definitions, assumptions, theorems and Appendix C proofs are substantively retained. v4 Appendix B.4.2 adds a Gaussian-prior/decimation setup and a closed-form MAP expression (Equation 25). As printed, its zero-mean conditional likelihood is inconsistent with the stated nonzero MAP formula.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion extend the empirical success claims to sparse-view CT. The central claims concerning single-operator self-supervision, the equivariance definition and MMSE optimality retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive guidance on transformation choice and approximate invariance, interprets near-equivariant operators as a failure condition, and discusses noise-misspecification stability and computational tradeoffs (Appendices A.2 and B.4). However, its blanket claim that ES outperforms EI with unknown noise conflicts with the high-noise MRI results in Table 8.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-availability link, reproducibility statement, training/inference pseudocode, an explicit 0.8 split ratio, ten inference samples, additional processing details and per-method timing/epoch information. These substantially expand disclosure without establishing changes to the core procedure. Table 10's ES MRI timing implies about 92 hours, conflicting with the retained 50-hour maximum.

R1.justification: v4 adds Armato III et al. (2011) for LIDC-IDRI, Portilla and Simoncelli (2000) for texture distributions, and Xu et al. (2016) for push-broom acquisition. The relationship to splitting, equivariant imaging and equivariant-network research, including the principal novelty claims, remains essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall section sequence are retained. v4 makes localized explanatory rewrites, particularly for forward operators, subdivides Appendix A, expands the metrics discussion, introduces additional appendix subheadings and adds a reproducibility statement. This is a limited narrative reorganization rather than a pervasive rewrite.

P2.justification: Table 1 expands from one MRI panel to three medical-imaging panels. New Tables 5 and 7-10 display transformation guidance, mask/noise analyses, MAP validation and timings, while Algorithms 1-2 add pseudocode blocks. Figures 1-8 retain their content with several relocations; v1 Table 5 becomes v4 Table 6. The evidence displays are substantially expanded.

improvement.justification: Acquired-MRI validation and targeted mask/noise tests substantially strengthen the evidence for practical applicability and reveal failure conditions absent from v1's evaluation. Explicit training/inference instructions and reported code access also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized defects in the additions: the overstated unknown-noise comparison in Table 8, inconsistent timing documentation and the likelihood/formula mismatch in the MAP example.
